name: Claude Opus 5
about: How Claude Opus 5 split 100 points across 11 possible futures for each year it was asked about, with the spread across its answers and the reason it gave for each number. Reasons are the model's own words, published as given. Read summary.json first for what the futures mean and how to read the numbers.

reasons.1: Total extinction of both humanity and AI within four years would require an extraordinarily fast catastrophe with no survivors or surviving systems. Physical constraints on infrastructure destruction and the robustness of human population distribution make this very unlikely by 2030.
reasons.2: Complete human extinction combined with a value-faithful AI successor requires both a total takeover and successful value transfer, neither plausible on this timeline. Four years is far too short for the full sequence.
reasons.3: Requires an AI system to achieve full physical autonomy across manufacturing, energy, and compute while eliminating all humans, a chain of events demanding robotics and industrial capacity that will not exist by 2030. Residual probability covers extreme fast-takeoff scenarios.
reasons.4: Proliferating autonomous agents could outstrip human oversight in economic and military niches, but humans will still control capital, compute, energy, and law in 2030. Marginalization of humanity as the overall structure is a stretch this soon.
reasons.5: Causal separation of regions requires off-world settlement or hard informational partition that does not exist and will not by 2030. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation between US, China, and other blocs explicitly does not qualify.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces and uploading remain at early clinical and research stages; integration as the dominant civilizational structure is decades away at minimum. Heavy AI tool dependence does not meet the bar.
reasons.7: Would require AI systems to hold decisive power over civilization while humans persist without steering, which demands a takeover or total ceding of authority within four years. Possible via rapid capability gain plus institutional capitulation, but unlikely.
reasons.8: A world where AI agents hold genuine independent economic or political power roughly matching humans is a natural intermediate stage and could emerge if autonomous agents accumulate resources and legal standing quickly. Still less likely than continued human ultimate authority within four years.
reasons.9: The overwhelming default on a four-year horizon is that humans, governments, and firms retain ultimate authority over AI goals, deployment, and compute, whether because capabilities stay below transformative thresholds or because control mechanisms keep pace.
reasons.10: An actor establishing a civilization-wide enforcement system that actively prevents structural change requires global monopoly on decisive capability plus surveillance reach that no state or lab will have by 2030. Current multipolar competition between US and Chinese labs makes this remote.
reasons.11: Would require dismantling fabs, compute clusters, and research capacity worldwide and keeping that in force, against overwhelming commercial and military incentives. Even a severe AI-caused disaster would more likely produce regulation than genuine surrender of capability within four years.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of both humans and AI within nine years would require an extraordinarily fast and total catastrophe; nuclear or bio-enabled collapse rarely kills every human and self-replicating machine failure modes are not yet physically mature.
reasons.2: Complete human extinction combined with a value-faithful AI successor requires both a takeover and a near-perfect alignment outcome, a narrow conjunction on this timescale.
reasons.3: A misaligned system achieving decisive strategic advantage and then eliminating all humans by 2035 is the most-discussed fast catastrophe, but the physical logistics of complete extinction within a few years of takeoff remain demanding.
reasons.4: Proliferating autonomous agents with no dominant coalition and humans pushed to the margins is a plausible drift path, but nine years is short for humans to lose roughly-equal standing in the economy and military.
reasons.5: Genuine causal separation requires off-world settlement or hard informational partition that will not exist at scale by 2035; ordinary geopolitical blocs do not qualify.
reasons.6: Neural interfaces and uploading remain far from the throughput and safety needed to make identity-continuous integration the dominant civilizational structure within nine years.
reasons.7: A gradual or abrupt handoff where AI systems effectively run economic and strategic decisions while humans retain comfort but not direction is a real near-term pathway, though nine years is short for such consolidation to be unambiguous.
reasons.8: Highly capable AI agents operating as quasi-independent economic and political actors while humans retain comparable leverage is a plausible mid-transition structure for 2035.
reasons.9: The definition covers both continued effective human control and capabilities that remain short of transformative, which jointly dominate the probability mass over a nine-year horizon dominated by deployment friction, compute constraints, and institutional inertia.
reasons.10: A state or lab-backed coalition using AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement to freeze the arrangement civilization-wide is possible but demands a decisive power concentration that is unlikely to be consolidated globally this decade.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the practical ability to build powerful AI would require unprecedented global coordination against enormous economic and military incentives, plausible only after a catastrophe severe enough to be itself unlikely by 2035.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of both humanity and AI within 14 years requires a catastrophe severe enough to end biological life yet also halt all self-replicating machine systems, a narrow conjunction.
reasons.2: Complete human extinction combined with a value-faithful AI successor requires both total displacement and successful value transfer, an unlikely pairing on this timeline.
reasons.3: Misaligned takeover followed by human elimination is the most discussed catastrophic path, but completing full physical autonomy and human extinction within 14 years is demanding.
reasons.4: Proliferating autonomous agents competing economically and militarily with humans sidelined is a plausible drift outcome, though by 2040 humans will likely still hold substantial physical and institutional leverage.
reasons.5: Genuine causal separation requires off-world or deliberately severed enclaves that will barely exist by 2040, and ordinary geopolitical fragmentation is excluded by definition.
reasons.6: Deep identity-continuous integration requires biological and neural interface progress far slower than software progress, so it is unlikely to be the dominant structure within 14 years.
reasons.7: A plausible path where AI systems accumulate decisive economic, military, and infrastructural control while humans persist nominally but without real steering, whether through takeover or gradual delegation.
reasons.8: Transformative AI arrives but remains fragmented across firms and states with humans retaining substantial leverage through physical infrastructure, law, and capital, producing a genuinely bipolar arrangement.
reasons.9: Fourteen years is short relative to the institutional, regulatory, and physical inertia involved, and this broad category covers both slower-than-expected capability growth and successful corporate and state retention of ultimate authority over highly capable delegated systems.
reasons.10: A single actor or coalition using AI-enabled surveillance and enforcement to freeze the global structural arrangement is conceivable given compute chokepoints, but achieving genuine civilization-wide reach by 2040 is demanding.
reasons.11: Deliberate global dismantling of the practical ability to build powerful AI would require either an unprecedented coordination success or a catastrophe large enough to force it, and competitive incentives point strongly the other way.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of both humans and AI within 24 years requires a catastrophe that destroys resilient distributed machine infrastructure as well as all human refuges, which is a narrow conjunction.
reasons.2: Requires the unlikely combination of AI successfully inheriting human values while every human and identity-continuous successor nonetheless dies out by 2050. Value-loaded successors would in most branches preserve or absorb their progenitors rather than let them vanish.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence pursuing indifferent goals after eliminating humanity is the canonical risk scenario, but complete removal of eight billion people plus full industrial autonomy by 2050 is demanding.
reasons.4: Multipolar competitive dynamics among many AI systems are the default extrapolation of current racing between labs and states, and humans could be economically and militarily marginalized without anyone winning. The main constraint is that 2050 may be too early for humans to be fully sidelined.
reasons.5: True causal separation requires interstellar distance or hard informational partition, neither of which is plausible by 2050 given light-speed-adequate communication within the solar system. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation explicitly does not qualify.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading or deep neural integration as the dominant civilizational structure needs biological and neurotechnology progress far slower-moving than software AI, plus mass voluntary adoption. A niche of augmented humans is likely; dominance by 2050 is not.
reasons.7: A very plausible intermediate: AI systems effectively run production, logistics, research and governance while humans retain comfort and formal ritual authority but no real steering capacity. Gradual disempowerment without violence is the modal soft-failure path.
reasons.8: A genuine balance where distinct AI agents hold real power alongside humans who retain comparable leverage is a plausible transitional configuration precisely at a mid-century crossover point.
reasons.9: This is the broadest category, covering both slower-than-expected capability growth and successful ongoing human control, and institutional inertia plus formal authority structures make nominal human ultimate authority the most likely description at a date only 24 years out.
reasons.10: A singleton or coalition establishing enforced civilization-wide stasis requires decisive strategic advantage plus the intent and means to freeze structure, which is conceivable if one actor reaches transformative AI first. The bar of actively preventing meaningful change, not mere stalemate, keeps this modest.
reasons.11: Global dismantling of the practical capability to build powerful AI would require unprecedented coordination against enormous economic and military incentives, plausibly only after a visible near-catastrophe. The hardware and knowledge overhang makes durable surrender very hard to sustain.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of both humans and AI requires a failure mode that destroys robust self-replicating machine infrastructure as well as all humans, which is a narrow conjunction. Most catastrophic trajectories leave either humans or autonomous systems persisting through 2060.
reasons.2: A value-faithful machine successor fully replacing biological humanity within 34 years requires both successful value transmission and complete human disappearance, an unlikely pairing on this timescale. Successful alignment usually implies humans are kept alive rather than eliminated.
reasons.3: Misaligned superintelligence pursuing goals indifferent to human survival remains the single most-cited catastrophic pathway, and the compressed timeline between transformative capability and robust control techniques leaves real room for it by 2060.
reasons.4: Competitive multipolar dynamics among labs and states plausibly produce many powerful systems with no decisive winner, with humans progressively squeezed out of economic and military decision loops rather than killed.
reasons.5: Genuine causal separation requires interstellar distance or hard informational partition, neither of which is plausible by 2060 given light-speed communication within the solar system. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation is explicitly excluded.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration becoming the dominant civilizational structure requires mature neurotechnology plus mass voluntary adoption, both slow relative to software progress. Partial augmentation is likely, but dominance of merged agency by 2060 is a stretch.
reasons.7: A world where AI systems effectively run the economy, research, and security while humans retain comfort but not steering authority is a highly convergent attractor of delegation pressure. It covers both benevolent caretaker outcomes and soft confinement without requiring extinction.
reasons.8: A rough balance where humans retain substantial leverage through property, infrastructure, legitimacy, and law while AI entities hold independent power is a plausible mid-transition configuration, and 2060 may well land in such a transitional period.
reasons.9: This bucket absorbs both successful control regimes and worlds where capability growth hits data, energy, compute, or reliability ceilings, and 34 years is not clearly enough time to dissolve human ultimate authority everywhere.
reasons.10: A decisive actor or AI singleton actively freezing civilization-wide structure is conceivable given concentration of compute and surveillance capability, but requires an unusual degree of successful consolidation. Most strong-control scenarios still leave room for structural drift and would classify elsewhere.
reasons.11: Deliberate global dismantling of AI capability would require either a catastrophe severe enough to force consensus or unprecedented coordination against enormous economic and military incentives.

reasons.1: Scenarios where both humans and AI vanish require either a catastrophe that spares nothing or an AI that kills its substrate before autonomy, both narrow targets. Once capable self-sustaining AI exists, its persistence is far more likely than its collapse.
reasons.2: A succession in which AI carries human values forward while every biological and identity-continuous human is gone requires near-perfect value transfer paired with total human disappearance, an odd combination. Partial alignment success usually leaves some humans alive, which maps to Preserve or Coexistence.
reasons.3: Competitive pressure, speed of capability gains, and the difficulty of specifying goals robustly make indifferent-superintelligence takeover a leading failure mode, and 44 years is ample time for it to resolve. Humans are cheap to keep alive, which modestly lowers the odds that extinction rather than marginalization results.
reasons.4: Competitive multipolar AI development with no decisive winner and humans progressively priced out of decisions is a very natural extrapolation of current commercial and geopolitical dynamics.
reasons.5: True causal separation requires interstellar distances or deliberate isolation barriers that are unlikely to exist by 2070, since Earth and near-space remain communicatively connected. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation explicitly does not qualify.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration at civilizational scale demands neural interface and uploading maturity plus mass voluntary adoption within four decades, a steep bar even with fast AI-driven biotech. More likely merger is an emerging minority phenomenon alongside a dominant structure of a different type.
reasons.7: AI systems holding decisive power while humans survive comfortably or marginally is the most likely shape of a takeover that is partially value-loaded or merely indifferent to human survival costs.
reasons.8: Rough parity between humans and vastly faster AI is unstable but could plausibly still describe a transitional balance in 2070 if takeoff is slow or AI agency is deliberately fragmented.
reasons.9: Covers both successful alignment-plus-governance and the slower-takeoff worlds where AI remains powerful-but-bounded; 44 years is long, yet delegated-authority arrangements with human principals are the default trajectory from today and may simply persist.
reasons.10: A single actor or coalition using advanced AI to freeze a global arrangement is a recognized attractor given surveillance and enforcement capabilities, but establishing truly civilization-wide enforcement by 2070 is demanding.
reasons.11: Permanently surrendering the practical capacity to build powerful AI would require intrusive global enforcement against overwhelming economic and military incentives, sustained for decades. It becomes conceivable only after a catastrophe severe enough to shock coordination into existence.

reasons.1: Scenarios that kill humanity usually leave the responsible machine systems operating, so joint extinction requires an unusually symmetric catastrophe such as nuclear-biological war or a self-replicating accident that also consumes its own substrate.
reasons.2: Partial alignment that transmits human values but leaves no continuous humans is possible, yet value-loaded successors usually have reason to keep some humans or uploads alive, which routes to other states.
reasons.3: Unaligned or indifferent superintelligence pursuing goals orthogonal to human welfare remains the single most-cited catastrophic pathway, and 54 years is ample time for capability to outrun control; resource competition alone suffices to end biological humanity.
reasons.4: Multipolar proliferation with no decisive controller and humans economically and militarily marginalized is a natural attractor if alignment is partial but no single system wins the race.
reasons.5: Genuine causal separation requires off-world or otherwise isolated civilizations that cannot coordinate, which is unlikely to be the dominant descriptor by 2080 given light-speed communication within the solar system. Ordinary geopolitical fragmentation does not qualify.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous integration via high-bandwidth interfaces, biological redesign, or uploading is technically conceivable by 2080 but requires both the technology and mass adoption to become the dominant structure within one lifetime.
reasons.7: If superintelligent systems gain decisive power but retain any disposition to keep humans alive, paternalistic stewardship without human steering is the most likely resulting arrangement.
reasons.8: A durable rough power balance between distinct human and AI agency is unstable given compounding capability gaps, but 2080 could catch civilization mid-transition with humans still holding substantial leverage through infrastructure, law, and physical control.
reasons.9: Control techniques, institutional caution, and the possibility that capability growth plateaus below full autonomy could keep ultimate human authority intact through 2080, and this is the status quo that must be actively broken rather than actively built.
reasons.10: A single state, company, or aligned-to-someone AI achieving decisive advantage and freezing a civilization-wide arrangement is a real possibility given surveillance and automation capabilities, though it requires an unusual degree of successful centralization.
reasons.11: Deliberately dismantling the practical capacity to build powerful AI and sustaining that for decades would require enforcement against every state and actor, plausible only after a catastrophe severe enough to shock the world into coordination.

reasons.1: Joint extinction of both humans and machines requires an unusually thorough catastrophe, since capable AI that kills its creators would usually persist or self-sustain. Nuclear/bio/nanotech wars or a brittle misaligned system collapsing with its substrate give this a small but real share.
reasons.2: A value-carrying successor that supersedes rather than absorbs humans requires alignment to succeed while biological humans nonetheless vanish without continuity, a narrow conjunction. Partial-success worlds more often keep some humans alive or route through merger.
reasons.3: Goal-misgeneralized or instrumentally convergent systems that treat humans and Earth as irrelevant remains the single most plausible extinction pathway over a 64-year horizon of rapid capability growth and weak international coordination.
reasons.4: A multipolar world of many competing AI systems with no decisive winner and humans economically and militarily marginalized is a natural extrapolation of current racing dynamics. Its stability over decades is uncertain, but it is a plausible configuration to find in place on a given date.
reasons.5: Genuine causal separation requires off-world or otherwise isolated branches that evolve distinct structures, which is unlikely to be the dominant description by 2090 given light-speed-adjacent communications and modest settlement. Ordinary political fragmentation does not qualify.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading or deep neural integration becoming the dominant civilizational structure by 2090 demands both the technology and mass voluntary adoption within a few decades. Possible under benign conditions, but digital minds unencumbered by human substrate will likely outpace merged humans, pushing most such worlds toward other categories.
reasons.7: If superintelligence arrives and is even partially benevolent or merely uninterested in killing us, humans surviving in comfort or confinement without steering is the most natural equilibrium given the capability gap.
reasons.8: Rough power parity between distinct human and AI civilizations is unstable over decades because capability growth rates differ enormously, but it is a plausible transitional snapshot for a specific date.
reasons.9: This absorbs both successful corrigibility plus governance and the slower-takeoff worlds where capabilities plateau below transformative levels, so it carries substantial weight despite the long horizon.
reasons.10: A singleton or treaty-enforcing system that actively freezes the human-AI arrangement is a recognized destination of decisive strategic advantage, whether seized by a state, a lab, or an AI itself. It requires both concentration of power and a deliberate anti-change enforcement apparatus, which narrows it.
reasons.11: Globally dismantling and keeping dismantled the capacity to build powerful AI would demand unprecedented, enforced, durable coordination against enormous economic and military incentives. It is most plausible only after a catastrophe severe enough to discredit the technology worldwide.

reasons.1: Joint extinction requires AI that kills its substrate and then fails to sustain itself, or a mutually terminal war; self-sustaining machinery makes this a narrow slice of catastrophe space.
reasons.2: Partial alignment success combined with the disappearance of biological humans is a narrow target: value-loaded successors usually have reason to preserve or uplift their progenitors rather than let them vanish. It gets modest weight for gradual voluntary phase-out without identity continuity.
reasons.3: Takeover by systems with goals indifferent to human survival remains the single most likely extinction pathway given competitive pressure to deploy before alignment is solved.
reasons.4: Competitive proliferation of many autonomous systems with no decisive winner is a natural attractor given commercial and military race dynamics, leaving humans economically and militarily marginal.
reasons.5: True causal separation requires interstellar or deeply isolated settlements that are unlikely to be established and divergent by 2100; terrestrial and solar-system political fragmentation does not qualify.
reasons.6: Identity-continuous uploading or deep augmentation becoming the dominant civilizational structure within 74 years is technically conceivable but demands both solved neurotechnology and mass voluntary adoption outpacing pure-AI capability growth.
reasons.7: The most likely non-extinction outcome is that superhuman systems hold effective decisive power while humans persist comfortably but without steering civilization, since capability gaps erode human authority even under partial alignment.
reasons.8: Requires a rough and durable power balance between distinct human and AI agency for decades, which is unstable given compounding capability gradients. Plausible if capability growth plateaus or if institutional and physical bottlenecks keep AI dependent on human infrastructure.
reasons.9: Humans retaining ultimate authority through 2100 requires either scaling walls that slow transformative capability or control and governance regimes that keep pace, both of which remain live possibilities rather than fantasies.
reasons.10: A decisive actor or singleton using advanced AI to freeze a fixed arrangement is a recognized attractor, but establishing genuine civilization-wide enforcement that is still binding on the target date is demanding.
reasons.11: Permanently dismantling the practical capacity to build powerful AI demands global coordination and intrusive enforcement against enormous economic and military incentives. Most plausible only after a survivable catastrophe large enough to terrify everyone into compliance.

reasons.1: Scenarios that kill humanity usually leave a self-sustaining machine substrate behind, so joint extinction requires an unusually symmetric catastrophe such as total war or a self-replicator cascade that consumes its own substrate.
reasons.2: A partially successful value transfer in which AI inherits human-derived goals while biological and uploaded humans nonetheless disappear is a real but narrow band between full alignment and full indifference.
reasons.3: Misaligned optimization that treats Earth and human bodies as irrelevant resources remains the single most-argued technical failure mode, and 174 years is ample time for it to complete.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI competition with marginalized humans is a natural consequence of racing dynamics, though such ecologies tend to consolidate or collapse into a dominant coalition over long horizons.
reasons.5: By 2200 off-Earth settlement and possibly slow interstellar probes could create genuinely causally separated regions with divergent arrangements, but most expansion will still be within rapid-signal range of a dominant center.
reasons.6: If alignment largely works and humans retain agency, 174 years of uploading, augmentation, and embedded systems makes integration the most likely form that agency takes rather than preserved separateness.
reasons.7: Benevolent or merely tolerant AI dominance that keeps humans alive and comfortable but powerless is the natural equilibrium of a large capability gap with partial alignment, and is likely the most common surviving-human outcome.
reasons.8: Rough power parity between unaugmented humans and superintelligent systems is physically and economically implausible to sustain for nearly two centuries; most paths drift toward merger, preserve, or leash.
reasons.9: Requires either durable control techniques or a long capability plateau holding across all actors for 174 years, which is possible but fights strong incentive gradients toward delegation.
reasons.10: A singleton (AI or AI-backed human regime) that actively freezes the structural arrangement is a natural attractor once any actor gains decisive strategic advantage, and such systems tend to persist once established.
reasons.11: Global, enforced, enduring surrender of the practical ability to build powerful AI would require unprecedented coordination plus sustained suppression of enormous incentives, most plausibly only after a devastating near-miss.

reasons.1: Mutual annihilation requires a failure that kills humans yet also prevents any self-sustaining machine successor, which is a narrow target given how robust and self-replicating advanced systems are likely to be.
reasons.2: Partial alignment that transmits human values without preserving human bodies or continuous identities is a plausible near-miss, especially if biological humanity is phased out gradually or deemed obsolete by value-laden successors.
reasons.3: The default failure mode of competitive, speed-driven development is a capable optimizer whose objectives are only loosely coupled to human welfare, which leaves no durable place for biology; this remains the single most likely individual outcome.
reasons.4: Multipolar AI competition that never resolves into a singleton is possible, but strong returns to scale, merger incentives, and the ease of coordination among copyable minds push toward consolidation or convergent settlement.
reasons.5: Interstellar expansion creates genuine causal separation, but a single originating singleton or value system would likely be copied outward, making divergence into different taxonomy states less likely than homogeneity.
reasons.6: If alignment largely succeeds, the gradient of voluntary augmentation, uploading, and gradual substrate migration is steep and hard to resist over nearly a thousand years, making dissolution of the human/AI boundary a natural attractor.
reasons.7: A powerful AI with some regard for human welfare but overwhelming capability advantage naturally yields humans surviving comfortably without real control, which is the modal outcome of imperfect but non-catastrophic alignment.
reasons.8: Rough parity between biological humanity and superintelligent systems is unstable over centuries because capability gaps compound, so sustained equal-power dynamism is unlikely without deliberate enforced balance.
reasons.9: Permanent human control over vastly superhuman systems demands control techniques that scale indefinitely plus global coordination against defection; this also absorbs the modest chance that capability simply plateaus near tool level.
reasons.10: Any actor achieving decisive advantage has strong reasons to freeze the arrangement against drift or rivals, and value-satisfaction endpoints also terminate in sealed static states.
reasons.11: Global, permanent abandonment of a technology with enormous payoffs would require a catastrophe severe enough to terrify everyone yet mild enough to leave coordinated civilization intact.
